phonemes.desc: Diphthong [ao] opening with [a] and gliding to [o] — the sacred first syllable, stressed.
Voiced bilabial nasal [m], the single consonant of the name.
Short open [a], the final vowel of the Avestan form 𐬵𐬀𐬊𐬨𐬀.

pronunciation.approximation: HAH-oh-mah — three light syllables, the stress on the first; no English vowel is exactly right for the 'ao' glide.

kin.label: Vedic Sanskrit
kin.form: Soma — the same deified pressed plant of the Rigveda, from the shared root *sewH- 'to press'

kin.label: Middle Persian
kin.form: Hōm — the sacramental plant of the Sasanian liturgy, still named in the Persian Rivayats

kin.label: Meaning
kin.form: Avestan haoma, 'the pressed one', from hu- 'press, extract the juice' (Bartholomae, AirWb)

pronunciation.note: Haoma is Tier-2: the restoration is plain ASCII, so the name's richness is semantic, not orthographic — 'the pressed one' names at once the plant, the god, and the rite.

domains.title: Haoma
domains.subtitle: Sacred Plant
domains.lead: Haoma is the deified sacred plant of Zoroastrianism, pressed at the dawn liturgy into the draught that grants vigor, wisdom, and a share in immortality. Green and golden-eyed, hymned as a yazata in his own right, he is the tradition's living sacrament — god, offering, and medicine crushed in a single mortar — and the Iranian double of the Vedic soma.

cards.name: The First Pressing
cards.desc: On the heights of Hara the green, golden-eyed plant was first pressed — the primordial sacrament of the Avesta (Yašt 9.16).

cards.name: Right Pressing, Wrong Pressing
cards.desc: Zarathuštra reproaches Haoma for the draught of the false priests; the plant answers with a roll of righteous pressers (Yasna 9.3–8).

cards.name: The Visionary Draught
cards.desc: For King Vīštāspa's hundredfold sacrifice, Haoma grants foreknowledge of the war and 'the most victorious of weapons' (Yašt 9.26).

cards.name: The Living Yasna
cards.desc: The nightly pounding of twigs with water and milk — performed for millennia, and still performed today (Yasna 9–11).

symbols.name: The green stalk with golden eyes
symbols.meaning: His Avestan self-description — the mountain herb that is simultaneously a god (Yašt 9.19)

symbols.name: The mortar and pestle
symbols.meaning: The pounding-stone of the Yasna, where god, offering, and congregation meet nightly (Yasna 9–11)

symbols.name: The white haoma (parahōm)
symbols.meaning: The paradisal plant of the renovation, drunk by the resurrected that they shall not die again (Bundahišn 30)

symbols.name: Spring water and milk
symbols.meaning: The two companions of the pressing — purity and nourishment joined in the consecrated draught

symbols.name: Mount Hara (Alborz)
symbols.meaning: The cosmic axis where the first pressing happened and Mithra keeps his watch — the sacrament's original altar (Yašt 9.16; 10.13)

mythology.lead: Haoma's mythology is liturgical before it is narrative: a plant so holy it became a god, hymned in his own Yašt, interrogated by Zarathuštra, granted to kings for victory, and pressed fresh every night of the year. His stories cluster around the mortar — the one altar that has never been abandoned.

myths.title: Haoma Who Was First Pressed
myths.text: The ninth Yašt is the hymn of the plant made god: Haoma, green and with golden eyes, who was first pressed on the heights of Hara (Yašt 9.16, 19). The Avesta remembers him as both herb and yazata — the only deity of the Iranian pantheon who is simultaneously the offering itself, pounded fresh on the pestle each night in the Yasna. His first-pressing on Hara Berezaiti, the Alborz, the axis of the world, is the same mountain where Mithra keeps his thousand-eared, thousand-eyed watch (Yašt 10.13) — sacrament and covenant share one summit. His color and eyes passed into iconography: the golden-green plant appears on Sasanian silver among the emblems of the consecrated banquet. Haoma collapses the distance between altar and deity: the offering does not merely represent the god — it is the god, crushed to give life.

myths.title: Zarathustra's Reproach and the Roll of the Righteous
myths.text: The most human scene in the Avesta opens the ninth chapter of the Yasna. Zarathuštra reproaches the plant: the karpans and the kavis — the sacrificial guilds he condemns — pressed you, Haoma, for the stupefying draught, and the plant stands accused by its own prophet (Yasna 9.1–3). Haoma answers with a catalogue of the righteous who pressed him rightly: Yima, who won the sun; Thraētaona, who struck down the three-mouthed Aži Dahāka; Kərəsāspa, who slew the horned dragon Gandarəβa; and Vīštāspa, who first confessed the good religion (Yasna 9.3–8). The exchange is unique — a prophet interrogating his own sacrament — and its verdict is exact: The scene gives the tradition its own charter myth of ritual reform, rare in the ancient world. the plant is holy; the abuse is in the pressing. Ritual ethics, not chemistry, decides what a sacrament does to the soul.

myths.title: The Draught of Vīštāspa
myths.text: For King Vīštāspa, Haoma was oracles and victory. In Yašt 9 the king offers the plant the sacrifice of a hundred stallions, a hundred oxen, a hundred rams, and a hundred loads of grain — and the hymn says Haoma grants him what armies could not buy: the most fortunate of thoughts and the most victorious of weapons, with foreknowledge of the coming war against the Turanians and their daeva-worshipping king Arjāsp (Yašt 9.26–30). When Vīštāspa drank the pressed haoma, his spirit was illumined and his enemies' devices laid bare; the same hymn remembers the plant's gifts of swift horses and vanquishing glory. The myth dignifies strategy as piety: the visionary draught makes foresight itself a weapon, and the patron king who drinks it fights with wisdom before he fights with armies.

myths.title: The Living Pressing
myths.text: The living pressing survives in the Yasna itself. Chapters 9 to 11 preserve the rite: the parahōm, the water of the spring, the milk, the pounding of the twigs while the priest sings the very stanzas of the ninth chapter; then the consecration, the offering to fire, and the sip shared by priest and congregation. Parsi priests perform a form of this liturgy daily to this day, pounding ephedra where the mountain plant of the hymns no longer grows — a substitution the tradition itself treats as legitimate, since the Avesta praises the plant pressed with purity, whatever its species. Where even one family of a village keeps the rite, the tradition counts the night as won for the good creation. A sacrament four thousand years old still rises, nightly, from a mortar — among the oldest continuously performed rituals on earth.

lore.syncretism: Haoma's double is the Vedic soma — the same root, the same deified press, the same golden-eyed herb sung as a god in the Rigveda's ninth maṇḍala. The parallel is so close that some verses translate almost line for line, and it anchors the soma–haoma problem: which plant? The Rigveda praises soma's mountains and rivers; the Avesta, haoma's; both press at dawn for a draught that grants vigor, cattle, and light to the mind. Yet the theologies diverge: Vedic soma is ambrosia for gods and poets, while the Avesta subjects haoma to an ethical audit — Zarathuštra himself reproaches the plant for its abuse by false priests. In Sasanian and later tradition Hōm retained his liturgical kingship; in Manichaean Iran his memory survived as the ritual cup's own name.
lore.culturalLegacy: The pressing never ended. Parsi priests in India and Zoroastrians in Iran still perform the Yasna nightly, pounding ephedra where the original mountain plant cannot be had; the botanical identity remains debated — the 'soma–haoma problem', argued from ephedra to harmel to psychoactive candidates. The name lives on as Hōm and Hom, a boy's name from Tehran to Mumbai, and in the month and day dedications of the Zoroastrian calendar. Few religious words travel further than this one: a plant-god pressed at dawn four millennia ago still answers at roll call.
lore.extendedMeditation: Haoma asks what a sacrament is. Not a symbol, exactly — the plant is eaten; not a drug alone — the ethics police it; not a metaphor — the god answers back. The rite's deepest claim is that matter can be holy without ceasing to be matter: water, twigs, milk, prayer, a mortar, a morning. In an age that splits body and meaning into separate compartments, Haoma's nightly chemistry lesson endures: what you take in shapes what you are, and a tradition that has blessed its breakfast for four thousand years knows something about slow transformation.
sources: Avesta, Yasna 9–11 (the Hōmāst, the pressing liturgy)
Boyce, Zoroastrians: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices
lore.archaeology: Haoma leaves no temple — his monument is the liturgy. But the soma–haoma debate ties him to material evidence: ephedra remains and pressing apparatus from Bronze Age Bactria–Margiana (the BMAC complex) have been read as soma/haoma paraphernalia, though the identification is contested. Avestan manuscripts from Iran and India transmit the ninth Yašt and the pressing chapters with their directions; Sasanian seals and silverwork show the ritual mortar and the banquet cup in aristocratic use. The modern fire temples of Yazd, Mumbai, and Karachi, where the pounding still sounds, are the cult's living site.
